stories.headline: Magyar launches EU reset diplomacy with Poland visit, Vienna talks, and Hungary-Ukraine minority rights consultations
stories.summary: Prime Minister Péter Magyar's first two foreign trips as PM — to Poland (May 19–20) and Vienna (May 21) — signaled a deliberate break from Orbán-era isolation. In Warsaw, Magyar met PM Tusk and President Nawrocki; in Vienna he met Chancellor Stocker, acknowledging an asbestos contamination issue from Austrian quarries affecting Hungarian municipalities. Separately, Hungarian and Ukrainian foreign ministers agreed to begin high-level consultations on ethnic Hungarian minority language rights in western Ukraine, with Magyar saying a Zelenskyy meeting could follow in June.

stories.headline: Pardon scandal reignited as new documents released, Magyar confronts Gulyás and Balog over K. Endre affair
stories.summary: New documents in the K. Endre pedophile-deputy pardon case — released first by the Magyar government then by President Sulyok's Sándor Palace — revealed that Balog Zoltán lobbied for the pardon and the presidential office's own chief of staff opposed it. Magyar publicly demanded Novák Katalin explain whether the Orbán family ordered the pardon; Fidesz faction leader Gulyás exchanged public messages with Magyar, and lawyer Gaudi-Nagy announced criminal and civil proceedings against the PM for allegedly linking him to the affair.

stories.headline: Tisza submits constitutional amendment to bar Orbán from ever returning as PM, Fidesz and EU officials warn of retroactivity concerns
stories.summary: The ruling Tisza Party submitted the Sixteenth Amendment to Hungary's Fundamental Law on May 20–21, which would cap prime ministers at eight years in office — retroactively applied, this permanently disqualifies Viktor Orbán, who served over 20 years in total. The amendment also provides for dissolving the Sovereignty Protection Office and restructuring public-interest foundations. Fidesz faction leader Gulyás rejected the proposal, accusing it of backdoor migration policy liberalization; EU officials were cited saying infringement proceedings may follow.

stories.headline: Magyar cuts political salaries by half and delivers first major TV interview outlining government's economic priorities
stories.summary: In his first prime ministerial interview (aired on RTL Saturday evening), Magyar announced deep cuts to salaries for ministers, MPs, mayors, and state company executives. His own PM salary will fall to HUF 3.8 million gross monthly — less than half of Orbán's. He also promised the HUF 100,000 school-start support for families in August and a SZÉP card payment for pensioners in autumn, and projected 2% GDP growth for 2026. Fidesz accused Magyar of inheriting an unfunded 2026 budget.

stories.headline: Tisza government appoints 55 state secretaries, completing new cabinet structure
stories.summary: President Sulyok signed the appointment of 55 state secretaries on May 24, on Magyar's recommendation, effective May 26. Magyar highlighted that one-third are women, the youngest is 28, and the appointees hold 103 degrees between them. Notable appointments include actor Nagy Ervin as culture state secretary, former Kongsberg arms company executive in defence, and Kálnoki Kis Attila (former 24.hu journalist and pentathlete) as sports state secretary.

stories.headline: MNB Governor Varga announces cooperation with Tisza government on euro adoption, addresses MNB foundations scandal
stories.summary: Hungarian National Bank Governor Mihály Varga gave multiple interviews across the week (including a podcast appearance and the Lámfalussy Conference opening address), signaling constructive cooperation with the new government on the euro adoption target of 2030, while calling it 'ambitious.' He confirmed ongoing investigation of Matolcsy-era MNB foundations, claimed over HUF 100 billion in savings already recovered, cited record FX reserves (€60bn) and 110 tonnes of gold, and said MNB will be a 'constructive partner' in meeting Maastricht criteria. He also noted the strong forint could create challenges for some exporters and said he is open to meeting PM Magyar.

stories.headline: Sulyok resists resignation pressure, attends Csíksomlyó Pentecost pilgrimage to public acclaim
stories.summary: President Tamás Sulyok — who faces demands from Magyar to resign by May 31 — traveled to Transylvania for the Csíksomlyó Pentecost pilgrimage (hundreds of thousands of attendees) and was greeted with sustained applause, which Fidesz-aligned media framed as popular endorsement. Legal experts debated removal mechanisms: some argued a parliamentary recall is possible without a constitutional amendment, while the Tisza government's plans to rewrite the constitution in full were described as the longer path. Sulyok has not resigned.
